newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada casts its eyes on Ford Canada for final deal.
newsitem.headline: Canada casts its eyes on Ford Canada for final deal.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers union will set its last strike deadline for the 1996 round of labor talks with the Big Three North American automakers on Monday, when it opens serious negotiations with Ford Motor Co. of Canada.

Ford Motor Co.'s Canadian arm is the last to sit across the table from Canada's largest private sector union and will be asked to meet a pattern settlement forged during talks with Chrysler Corp. and begrudgingly accepted by General Motors Corp. after a 20-day strike that ended last week.
CAW President Buzz Hargrove said the strike deadline at Ford will likely leave nine days for the two sides to come up with an agreement before a strike was called.
"It (the deadline) will probably be a week Wednesday," Hargrove said.
Last week the union ended a strike that shut down all its plants in Canada, idled 20,000 GM workers in the United States and Mexico and paralyzed parts suppliers across North America.

The three-year Canadian pact, which was ratified by the union membership on Wednesday, provides for the sale of two of GM's Ontario parts plants but includes a pledge by the automaker to freeze outside contracting of work, known as outsourcing, for the life of the deal.
The union, in turn, made a major concession by accepting that GM's business plan may require deviance from a pattern agreement reached in September with Chrysler.
Ford Canada has no major parts plants in Canada and is not expected to endure a strike over outsourcing provisions in the pattern agreement.

However, Ford officials declined to comment ahead of the start of talks on whether the automaker will seek to carve out its own concessions from the Chrysler pattern and whether it would be willing to endure a strike to do so.
In Canada, the union traditionally fashions a pattern agreement at one of the three automakers and then attempts to apply that pattern to the other two.
This year, the union said it recognized differences at General Motors from Ford and Chrysler because the company had already announced it would sell two of its parts plants in Canada be talks began.
Ford has one truck and van assembly plant, one car assembly plant, one engine assembly plant and a parts distribution plant in Canada, employing 11,690 CAW workers.
In the United States, talks between the United Auto Workers union and General Motors adjourned Saturday night ahead of a Sunday night deadline.
The UAW announced on Friday that it will terminate its extended 1993 contract with the automaker if the union's 11:59 p.m. EST Sunday (0459 GMT Monday) deadline passes with no agreement.
As in Canada, the major unresolved issues in the United States include GM's ability to outsource and the sale of two parts plants in Michigan.
UAW officials said the buyer for all four of the U.S. and Canadian plants was Joseph, Littlejohn and Levy, a New York-based investment firm that owns other auto parts firms.
